verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse.sanskrit: श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात् । स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम् ॥
verse.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.
verse.why: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.
verse.misuse: Not 'stick to the role you were born into'. It's about honest fit with your own nature, not caste or family script.

prasang.title: Duties by nature, and their fruit
prasang.summary: After listing duties by varna, Krishna says one reaches perfection through one's own work done as worship, and that one's own path, though imperfect, beats another's, since every undertaking has flaws.
prasang.lesson: Do the work that fits you, flaws and all, as an offering.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is frozen by doubt about what to do. Krishna tells him to focus on the work that matches his own nature. The work might have flaws. But doing your own duty, even if you do it poorly, is better than doing someone else's duty perfectly. The point is that you do not incur fault by doing what is truly yours.
verse.for_you: Your mother tells aunties you are exploring options. The shame of that feels heavy. But your own path, even in a café, is yours alone. Do not measure its worth against their desks at Goldman or Deloitte.

verse.speaker: Tulsidas
verse.setting: Tulsidas, introducing his work, on how rarely people rejoice at someone else's rise.
verse.sanskrit: जग बहु नर सर सरि सम भाई। जे निज बाढ़ि बढ़हि जल पाई॥ सज्जन सकृत सिंधु सम कोई। देखि पूर बिधु बाढ़इ जोई ॥
verse.line: Most of us swell only at our own rise. Rare is the one who surges at another's.
verse.translation: Brother, most people in the world are like ponds and rivers: they swell only when their own waters rise. Rare is the good soul who, like the ocean, surges with joy on seeing another's moon grow full.
verse.why: Notice whether you can be glad at someone else's good work, not only your own.

prasang.title: Tulsidas on loving our own work
prasang.summary: Tulsidas calls his own poetry plain and asks readers to forgive it. Along the way he notes that everyone loves their own work, that few are glad at another's success, and that most people swell only with their own rising waters.
prasang.lesson: Notice whether you can be glad at someone else's good work, not only your own.

verse.meaning: Tulsidas is writing the Ramcharitmanas and admits his own verse is plain. He says most people are like ponds and rivers, they swell only when their own waters rise. A rare soul is like the ocean, surging with joy at another's moon. He asks you to notice if you can feel glad at a friend's good work, not only your own.
verse.for_you: You are working in a café while friends are at Goldman and Deloitte. The flat whites are not the problem. It is the picture of them ahead that keeps replaying. Ask yourself if you can be glad at their good work, or if you can only swell at your own rise.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse.sanskrit: यदृच्छालाभसन्तुष्टो द्वन्द्वातीतो विमत्सरः । समः सिद्धावसिद्धौ च कृत्वापि न निबध्यते ॥
verse.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.
verse.why: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

prasang.title: How the great yogis live
prasang.summary: The wise act without selfish motive, content and dependent on nothing, free from envy, steady in success and failure.
prasang.lesson: Contentment and freedom from envy let you work without being bound.

verse.meaning: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna about how the wise live. He says that a person who is content with what comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, and free from envy, remains the same in success and failure, and is not bound even while acting. The wise act without selfish motive, content and dependent on nothing. You can hold that your worth is not measured by where your mates are.
verse.for_you: The café shifts and the applications you sent are your ground. Your worth is not measured by where your mates are. Hold that steady while it hurts.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
verse.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
verse.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
verse.why: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader about steadfastness. He says that the wise let others praise or blame them. They let money come or go. They let death come today or ages from now. The steady do not move a step from the right path.
verse.for_you: Your mother tells aunties you are exploring options. The café shifts are not the shame. The envy of your friends at Goldman and Deloitte is what keeps you from opening the app. The steady do not step off the path because others praise or blame.

verse.speaker: Dharmavyadha (the righteous meat-seller)
verse.setting: In Mithila, a meat-seller famed for wisdom teaches a proud ascetic what goodness really is.
verse.sanskrit: अनसूयुः कृतज्ञश्च कल्याणान्येव सेवते / सुखानि धर्ममर्थं च स्वर्गं च लभते नरः
verse.line: Let go of envy and stay grateful, and good things keep finding their way to you.
verse.translation: The person who is free of envy and grateful keeps to what is good, and finds happiness, right living, prosperity and heaven.
verse.why: Wisdom lives in ordinary people doing ordinary work honestly. Care for your parents.

verse.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
verse.setting: The sage warns the deposed prince against resenting others' success.
verse.sanskrit: सहस्व श्रियमन्येषां यद्यपि त्वयि नास्ति सा / अन्यत्रापि सतीं लक्ष्मीं कुशला भुञ्जते नराः / अभिनिष्यन्दते देही श्रीभूतश्च द्विषज्जनात्
verse.line: Make peace with other people's success, even when you lack it. The wise can enjoy good fortune that isn't theirs.
verse.translation: Bear the good fortune of others, even though it is not with you. Wise people know how to enjoy good fortune even when it belongs to someone else; good fortune drains away from the one who resents.
verse.why: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

prasang.title: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasang.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

verse.meaning: Kalakavrikshiya speaks to the deposed prince Kshemadarshi. The prince has lost his kingdom and wealth and is drowning in grief and envy. The sage tells him that sorrow cannot bring back what is gone. He says the wise know how to bear the good fortune of others without resentment. The sage says good fortune drains away from the one who resents, so the prince must want what is within his reach and make peace with the success of others.
verse.for_you: Walk your own path, even imperfectly, rather than someone else's well; be grateful for what is yours and rejoice in others' good.

story.title: Ram accepts exile
story.story_hook: He went to the palace to be crowned and came out with fourteen years in the forest.
story.summary: On the morning of his coronation, Ram is summoned and told by Kaikeyi that he must go into the forest for fourteen years. He agrees without anger, and is hurt only that his father could not tell him himself. He walks out showing no change of mind, already thinking of those he must comfort.
story.lesson: You cannot control the news; you can control the person who walks out of the room.

anchor.speaker: Narrator
anchor.setting: Ram walks out of the palace, having lost the throne he was to receive that morning.
anchor.sanskrit: न वनं गन्तुकामस्य त्यजतश्च वसुंधराम्। सर्वलोकातिगस्येव लक्ष्यते चित्तविक्रिया॥
anchor.line: He had just lost the kingdom, and his mind showed no change at all.
anchor.translation: As he set out for the forest and gave up the earth, no change could be seen in his mind, as if he stood beyond the world.
anchor.why: You cannot control the news; you can control the person who walks out of the room.
anchor.misuse: Calm in loss is not pretending it does not hurt; Ram grieves elsewhere in the story.

script: You sent out applications and you are working in a café. Your friends are at Goldman and Deloitte. You avoid LinkedIn. Your mother tells aunties you are exploring options. That shame sits with you. It feels like you are stuck.
Arjuna stands on a battlefield. He is frozen. He does not know if he should fight. Krishna looks at him. Arjuna has asked what his duty is. And Krishna replies:
श्रेयान्स्वधर्मो विगुणः परधर्मात्स्वनुष्ठितात्, स्वभावनियतं कर्म कुर्वन्नाप्नोति किल्बिषम्.
In plain words: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.

Krishna says to do the work born of your own nature. Even if it is imperfect. Even if it has flaws. That is better than doing someone else's work perfectly. This is because every undertaking has its own trouble. When you do your own work, you do not incur the wrong of taking on a burden that is not yours.

Your mother's words about exploring options sting. But your path is your own. It is the work you are doing. It is not their desks. It is not their titles. Your own imperfect work is your offering. You do not incur fault by doing what is truly yours.
What is your own path today.

depth.points: The texts say your own duty, even imperfectly done, is better than another's done perfectly. Your worth is not measured by their desks. The work you do now is your own.
depth.practice: Open the app you stopped using today. Look at one job posting without judging it.
depth.question: What would it look like to value your own path, even in a café?
